{{Short description|One of two types of graph}}
{{distinguish|book embedding}}
[[File:Graph book sample.gif|thumb|A triangular book]]
In [[graph theory]], a '''book graph''' (often written <math>B_p</math>&nbsp;) may be any of several kinds of graph formed by multiple cycles sharing an edge.

==Variations==
One kind, which may be called a '''quadrilateral book''', consists of ''p'' [[quadrilateral]]s sharing a common edge (known as the "spine" or "base" of the book). That is, it is a [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian product]] of a [[star (graph theory)|star]] and a single edge.<ref>{{mathworld|id=BookGraph|title=Book Graph}}</ref><ref name="gallian">{{cite journal
 | last = Gallian | first = Joseph A. | author-link = Joseph Gallian
 | journal = [[Electronic Journal of Combinatorics]]
 | mr = 1668059
 | page = Dynamic Survey 6
 | title = A dynamic survey of graph labeling
 | url = http://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/DS6
 | volume = 5
 | year = 1998}}</ref> The 7-page book graph of this type provides an example of a graph with no [[harmonious labeling]].<ref name="gallian"/>

A second type, which might be called a '''triangular book''', is the complete tripartite graph ''K''<sub>1,1,''p''</sub>.  It is a graph consisting of <math>p</math> [[triangle]]s sharing a common edge.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Lingsheng Shi |author2=Zhipeng Song |title=Upper bounds on the spectral radius of book-free and/or ''K''<sub>2,l</sub>-free graphs |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications |volume=420 |year=2007 |issue=2–3 |pages=526–9 |doi=10.1016/j.laa.2006.08.007|doi-access=free }}</ref>  A book of this type is a [[split graph]].  
This graph has also been called a <math>K_e(2,p)</math><ref>{{cite journal|last=Erdős|first=Paul|year=1963|title=On the structure of linear graphs|journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]|volume=1|issue=3 |pages=156–160|authorlink=Paul Erdős|doi=10.1007/BF02759702|doi-access=free}}</ref> or a '''thagomizer graph''' (after [[thagomizer]]s, the spiked tails of [[stegosauria]]n dinosaurs, because of their pointy appearance in certain drawings) and their [[graphic matroid]]s have been called thagomizer matroids.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gedeon|first=Katie R.|issue=3|journal=Electronic Journal of Combinatorics|mr=3691529|at=Paper 3.12|title=Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials of thagomizer matroids|volume=24|year=2017|doi=10.37236/6567 |s2cid=23424650 |arxiv=1610.05349}}; {{cite journal|last1=Xie|first1=Matthew H. Y.|last2=Zhang|first2=Philip B.|doi=10.1090/proc/14608|issue=11|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|mr=4011505|pages=4687–4695|title=Equivariant Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials of thagomizer matroids|volume=147|year=2019|doi-access=free|arxiv=1902.01241}}; {{cite journal|last1=Proudfoot|first1=Nicholas|last2=Ramos|first2=Eric|doi=10.1007/s00029-019-0509-4|issue=4|journal=Selecta Mathematica|mr=4021848|at=Paper 62|series=New Series|title=Functorial invariants of trees and their cones|volume=25|year=2019|arxiv=1903.10592|s2cid=85517485 }}</ref> Triangular books form one of the key building blocks of [[line perfect graph]]s.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Maffray | first = Frédéric
 | doi = 10.1016/0095-8956(92)90028-V
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
 | mr = 1159851
 | pages = 1–8
 | series = Series B
 | title = Kernels in perfect line-graphs
 | volume = 55
 | year = 1992| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

The term "book-graph" has been employed for other uses.  Barioli<ref>{{cite journal |first=Francesco |last=Barioli |title=Completely positive matrices with a book-graph |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications |volume=277 |year=1998 |issue=1–3 |pages=11–31 |doi=10.1016/S0024-3795(97)10070-2|doi-access=free }}</ref> used it to mean a graph composed of a number of arbitrary subgraphs having two vertices in common.  (Barioli did not write <math>B_p</math> for his book-graph.)

==Within larger graphs==
Given a graph <math>G</math>, one may write <math>bk(G)</math> for the largest book (of the kind being considered) contained within <math>G</math>.

==Theorems on books==
Denote the [[Ramsey number]] of two triangular books by <math>r(B_p,\ B_q).</math> This is the smallest number <math>r</math> such that for every <math>r</math>-vertex graph, either the graph itself contains <math>B_p</math> as a subgraph, or its [[complement graph]] contains <math>B_q</math> as a subgraph.

* If <math>1\leq q</math>, then <math>r(B_1,\ B_q)=2q+3</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Rousseau | first1 = C. C. | author1-link = Cecil C. Rousseau
 | last2 = Sheehan | first2 = J.
 | doi = 10.1002/jgt.3190020110
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Journal of Graph Theory]]
 | mr = 486186
 | pages = 77–87
 | title = On Ramsey numbers for books
 | volume = 2
 | year = 1978}}</ref>
* There exists a constant <math>c=o(1)</math> such that <math>r(B_p,\ B_q)=2q+3</math> whenever <math>q\geq cp</math>.
* If <math> p\leq q/6+o(q)</math>, and <math>q</math> is large, the [[Ramsey number]] is given by <math>2q+3</math>.
* Let <math>C</math> be a constant, and <math>k = Cn</math>.  Then every graph on <math>n</math> vertices and <math>m</math> edges contains a (triangular) <math>B_k</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |first=P. |last=Erdős |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ijm/1255631811 |title=On a theorem of Rademacher-Turán |journal=Illinois Journal of Mathematics |volume=6 |year=1962 |pages=122–7 |doi=10.1215/ijm/1255631811|doi-access=free }}</ref>
